lesson.title: Heuristics and simulated annealing
lesson.subtitle: Local search, local optima and temperature

video.title: Heuristics and simulated annealing: Local search, local optima and temperature

scenes.narration: The faculty must schedule six hundred exams into three weeks with no student sitting two at once. An exact solver runs all weekend and does not finish. A simple heuristic finds a clash-free timetable in a minute. Is it the best one?
Today: why some problems are too large for exact methods, how local search gets stuck, and how simulated annealing escapes by sometimes accepting worse moves.

Many scheduling and routing problems are NP-hard, so exact methods may take impossibly long on large instances. Heuristics trade the guarantee of optimality for good solutions found quickly. They need careful evaluation instead.

Local search starts from a solution and repeatedly moves to a better neighbour, for example by moving one exam to another slot. It stops when no neighbour is better. That point is a local optimum, which may be far from the best.

Simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse move, with probability e to the minus delta over T. At high temperature it explores freely. As T cools, it settles, and with slow enough cooling it can escape local optima.

A move that is worse by two is accepted with probability e to the minus two at temperature one, about fourteen percent. At temperature ten it is accepted about eighty two percent of the time. Cooling turns exploration into refinement.

Students often report one run of a heuristic and call it the answer. Require several runs with different seeds, a comparison with a lower bound or an exact solution on small instances, and a plot of cost against time.
Quick check! Local search stops with eight clashes left, and no single exam move reduces them. What has it found?
A local optimum. No neighbour is better, but a sequence of moves, some worse at first, might reach zero clashes.
In the app, open the annealing lab. Run local search and annealing on the same problem, change the starting temperature, and compare the final costs.
Your turn. At temperature two, how likely is annealing to accept a move that is worse by two?
About thirty seven percent: e to the minus one. Remember: local search finds local optima, annealing escapes by accepting some worse moves, and heuristics must be evaluated over many runs.
